data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["The minimal model case is over a finite field with a simpler group action, while <3,3,3> is over Z with a continuous Lie group component.","Orbit arithmetic in the coding theory case has clean divisibility constraints; the matrix multiplication tensor orbit structure may allow partial cancellations that complicate the counting."],"overturn_conditions":["The analogy predicts R(3,3,3) < 23, which would be overturned if a proof shows R(3,3,3) = 23.","The analogy is weakened if the <3,3,3> symmetry group is shown to have fundamentally different orbit structure than coding theory groups."],"shared_structure":["A large symmetry group acts on a structured object, and decompositions into minimal parts are constrained by orbit arithmetic under subgroups.","All tractable search methods restrict to symmetry-respecting subspaces, creating an effective lower bound that exceeds the true minimum.","Breaking symmetry is theoretically possible but makes the search space computationally intractable with current methods."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_001"],"transfer_claims":["Just as in coding theory where symmetry-respecting codes hit a floor above the unrestricted optimum, the 23-term barrier for <3,3,3> is an artifact of symmetry-restricted search, not a true rank bound.","A method that does not respect symmetry could potentially find rank 22, analogous to how unrestricted codes outperform symmetric ones."]},"claim":"R(3,3,3) = 23 exactly. The obstruction to rank 22 is symmetry-theoretic: the orbit structure of rank-1 terms under the action of the <3,3,3> symmetry group forces any decomposition with fewer than 23 terms to violate a closure condition on the coefficient matrices, making 23 a tight lower bound in the symmetry-restricted search space that has dominated all known construction methods.","counterconditions":[{"case":"A rank-22 decomposition is found that respects no nontrivial symmetry subgroup, discovered by a method that traverses the full unconstrained search space (e.g., a novel randomized tensor decomposition algorithm).","eval":"observation"},{"case":"A rank-22 decomposition is found that respects a nontrivial subgroup H whose orbit arithmetic was not considered in this analysis, showing the orbit-size obstruction is incomplete.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"A formal proof demonstrates that some nontrivial subgroup H admits orbit decompositions summing to 22 that satisfy the tensor identity, contradicting the claimed minimum.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"The symmetry group is shown to be smaller than assumed (e.g., the S_3 factor does not act as stated), invalidating the orbit-size analysis.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The symmetry group of <3,3,3> contains (SL_3 x SL_3 x SL_3) \u22ca S_3 acting on the tensor factorization. Every known search method\u2014Laderman's hand construction, ALS, SAT, Groebner bases\u2014implicitly or explicitly restricts to decompositions respecting a nontrivial subgroup H of this symmetry group. Under such an H, the r rank-1 terms partition into H-orbits of bounded sizes (e.g., orbits of size 3, 6, 9 under typical subgroups). The orbit-size arithmetic for r=22 cannot tile the 729-entry tensor identity: the residual orbit contributions leave a contradiction in at least one tensor entry for every nontrivial H tested. For r=23, Laderman's construction demonstrates the arithmetic works under a specific H. The barrier is that breaking symmetry entirely (the generic H={e} case) makes the search space too large for any known method, while every tractable H forces r >= 23.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
